**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Engineering Lead
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Date:** Internal — for discussion at Thursday's planning session

Over the past few weeks we've been circling the same question: our inference workloads are bumping against capacity during peak hours, queue times are creeping up, and the obvious instinct is to buy more hardware. I want to argue that the right move right now is the less obvious one — spend the next quarter seriously improving utilisation of the eight GPUs we already own, and revisit the purchase decision with real data in hand.

Let me start with the case for buying, because it's not a weak one. New hardware is simple. It arrives, we rack it, capacity goes up, and the p99 latency numbers we've been watching drift back under our SLO. There's no organisational effort involved, no risk of a half-finished optimisation project that delivers 60% of its promise. When a team is feeling capacity pain, simplicity has real value, and I don't want to dismiss that.

But the economics push the other way. The quote we got for the expansion is roughly equivalent to two full engineering salaries for a year, and that's before power, cooling, and the depreciation that hits the moment the boxes arrive. Meanwhile, our own telemetry tells a more interesting story than "we're out of capacity." Average utilisation across the fleet sits around 40%, with sharp peaks in the late morning and after dinner. That's not a capacity problem; that's a scheduling and batching problem. Our models are served one request at a time with conservative batch sizes, our least-used model occupies a dedicated card that sits idle most of the day, and we have no mechanism for pre-empting batch jobs when interactive traffic surges. If we can lift effective utilisation to 65 or 70% — which peer teams have done with comparable workloads — we buy ourselves the headroom we need without spending the capital budget.

There's also the question of what we'd be giving up. Two engineers spending a quarter on this purchase means a quarter not spent on the retrieval-quality work that product has been asking for, and that work has a clearer line to revenue than anything we'd rack in the closet. Opportunity cost is easy to ignore because it never shows up on an invoice, but it's the largest line item in this decision.

Latency deserves its own paragraph, because it's the strongest argument on the buy side and I want to address it honestly. Better batching and smarter scheduling do add small amounts of queuing delay by design — you're deliberately waiting a few milliseconds to fill a batch. Done well, that trade is overwhelmingly favourable: p50 latency may rise slightly while p99 improves dramatically, because we stop the head-of-line blocking that currently causes our worst tail behaviour. But done badly, aggressive batching can make tail latency worse, not better. This is a real risk and it's why I'm proposing we treat the effort as an engineering project with explicit latency budgets, not a background chore.

Reliability cuts both ways. More hardware means more redundancy, and I won't pretend otherwise — losing one of eight cards hurts less than losing one of four. But our current failure mode isn't hardware loss; it's the fact that our serving stack is so tightly coupled to specific devices that a single card failure takes a model offline until someone manually reassigns it. Fixing that — making placement dynamic and failure-aware — improves reliability *and* utilisation simultaneously. Buying more cards would leave that fragility untouched, just spread across a larger fleet.

Finally, reversibility. A purchase is a one-way door. Once the capital is spent and the depreciation schedule starts, we own that hardware whether or not our workload mix changes — and our workload mix has changed twice in the last year. The utilisation work is a two-way door: if it stalls or the results disappoint, we've lost a quarter of engineering time and we can still make the purchase with better information. If it succeeds, we may find we don't need the purchase at all, or that we need different hardware than we assumed.

So my recommendation: commit two engineers for one quarter to dynamic scheduling, model co-location, and batching improvements, with a hard gate at the end — if p99 latency under peak load isn't within 15% of our SLO, we escalate the hardware request immediately with my full support. I want to be clear that I'm not certain this works. Utilisation projects have a well-earned reputation for eating quarters and delivering half their promise. But the downside is bounded and known, the upside is substantial, and the alternative commits real capital on the basis of a utilisation number we haven't actually tried to move.

I'd like to walk through this together on Thursday. Please come with objections — especially from those of you closest to the serving stack, who will know best whether 65% is a fantasy or a floor.

**Internal Memo — To: Platform Engineering Team**
**From: Engineering Lead**
**Re: GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?**

I want to lay out my thinking on the capacity question we've been circling for the past few weeks, because I think we're closer to a decision than our discussions might suggest. The question, stated plainly: do we purchase additional local inference hardware, or do we invest in raising the utilisation of the machines we already own?

Let me start with the economics, because they're less ambiguous than they first appear. Our current fleet of accelerators is running at roughly 30–35% utilisation during business hours, and lower outside them. That number should give us pause before we spend anything. New hardware at our scale means a capital outlay in the low six figures once you include networking, rack space, power provisioning, and the engineering time to integrate and operate it. Against that, the utilisation work — better batching, request coalescing, a smarter scheduling layer, and honestly just instrumenting the fleet properly so we can see where the idle capacity actually sits — is a fraction of that cost, mostly paid in engineering time we'd spend anyway. The opportunity cost cuts both ways, of course: every week an engineer spends on the scheduler is a week not spent on the product roadmap. But the roadmap work we'd defer is incremental, while the capacity question, if we get it wrong in either direction, is expensive.

On latency, I want to be honest about the trade-off. The strongest argument for buying more hardware is that headroom is latency insurance. When the fleet is busy, queueing delays show up directly in p95 and p99 response times, and our users feel that before we do. A utilisation push that pushes average load from 35% to 70% will narrow that buffer, and we should expect some tail-latency degradation during spikes. My view is that this is manageable — modern batching and scheduling techniques let us run hot on throughput while keeping tail latencies within acceptable bounds — but "manageable" is doing real work in that sentence, and we should treat it as a hypothesis to be tested, not an assumption to be baked in.

Reliability is where the utilisation argument gets its second wind. Right now, a single hardware failure takes a meaningful slice of our capacity offline, and because our machines are individually underused, we've never had to think hard about failover. If we buy more hardware, we inherit more failure modes and more maintenance surface, and we'd be doing it before we've built the operational muscle to manage what we have. Paradoxically, running closer to capacity forces us to build the redundancy, graceful degradation, and load-shedding behaviours that make the whole system more robust. Those are capabilities we will need regardless of what we eventually buy.

The reversibility point is, for me, the decisive one. Buying hardware is a largely one-way door. Depreciation starts immediately, resale value is poor, and the commitment shapes our architecture and our budget for years. Improving utilisation is a reversible door: if the scheduling work stalls, if tail latencies degrade beyond what we can tolerate, or if demand grows faster than our optimisations can absorb, we can still buy hardware later, having lost only time and having gained a much sharper understanding of our true capacity needs. The option value of waiting is real, and it's currently free.

So my recommendation is this: we commit to a focused, time-boxed utilisation effort — roughly one quarter, with explicit latency and reliability targets — and we defer the purchase decision until we see the results. I'd frame the buy as the default fallback rather than the rejected option. If utilisation workplateaus above 60% with acceptable tail latencies, we've likely saved ourselves a significant capital outlay. If it doesn't, we'll buy, and we'll buy with data instead of anxiety.

I want to acknowledge the genuine uncertainty here. Demand forecasts are shaky, and there's a scenario — a large customer signing, a new product surface — where waiting costs us more than the hardware would. If anyone on the team sees that scenario as more likely than I do, I want to hear it before we lock this in. Let's discuss at Thursday's planning session, and if there's agreement, I'll draft the utilisation project brief this week.

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Engineering Lead
**Date:** Internal — for discussion at Thursday's planning session
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?

Over the past few weeks, several of you have raised the same question from different angles: our inference cluster is running hot, queue times during peak hours are creeping up, and we need to decide whether to purchase additional local hardware or invest in getting more out of the machines we already own. I want to lay out my thinking ahead of Thursday so we can have a productive debate rather than starting from scratch.

Let me start with the case that's easiest to quantify. Our current fleet of eight GPUs was purchased roughly eighteen months ago, and our own telemetry suggests average utilisation sits somewhere between 35 and 45 percent, with sharp peaks in the late morning and early evening. That gap between average and peak load is the crux of the whole decision. Buying more hardware would raise our ceiling, but it would also raise our floor of idle capacity, and idle silicon is pure depreciation. At current prices, a modest expansion would cost somewhere in the region of what we spend on cloud overflow in a year, and the payback period only makes sense if demand keeps growing at its recent trajectory. We believe it will, but "believe" is doing real work in that sentence.

The utilisation path, by contrast, is mostly an investment of engineering time rather than capital. Batching more aggressively, tightening our model quantisation, scheduling batch jobs into the overnight trough, and putting a proper priority queue in front of the cluster would plausibly lift effective utilisation into the 60 to 70 percent range. That is not free — it's maybe four to six weeks of focused work from two engineers, and it adds operational complexity that someone will have to own. But it attacks the actual problem, which is not that we lack capacity in aggregate; it's that our capacity is badly shaped relative to demand.

Latency is where the trade-off gets genuinely interesting. Right now, our p95 response times during peak are acceptable but not comfortable, and interactive workloads occasionally queue behind long-running batch jobs. Better scheduling fixes most of that at zero hardware cost. Additional hardware would also fix it, and would give us headroom for the latency-sensitive experiments we keep deferring. But there's an asymmetry worth noting: scheduling improvements make the system *smarter*, while more hardware just makes it *bigger*. Smarter systems keep paying dividends as we grow; bigger systems reset the problem at a higher level.

Reliability cuts in favour of the utilisation path too, though less decisively. Eight machines is already a small fleet, and a single hardware failure removes twelve percent of our capacity. Adding four more machines doesn't change that fragility much — it just makes each failure slightly less painful. What actually improves reliability is the operational maturity that comes with better scheduling and monitoring: knowing what's running, what it's worth, and what to shed first when something breaks. That said, I don't want to oversell this. More hardware does give us genuine redundancy for failover and lets us take a machine down for maintenance without sweating, and we currently can't do that gracefully.

The strongest argument for buying, in my view, is opportunity cost and reversibility — but it cuts both ways. If we spend six weeks on scheduling work and demand doubles anyway, we've delayed the inevitable purchase and lost time we could have spent on product work. Conversely, hardware is a semi-irreversible commitment: it depreciates, it consumes power and rack space, and if our workload shifts toward hosted models or a different accelerator architecture, we're stuck with sunk capital. Engineering time, spent on utilisation, is largely recoverable — the scheduling and batching infrastructure remains valuable regardless of how capacity evolves. In a period of genuine uncertainty about where our inference workloads are heading, I'd rather hold the reversible option.

So my recommendation is this: commit to a focused utilisation push over the next quarter, with a concrete trigger attached. If, after that work, our p95 peak latency still breaches our target, or utilisation exceeds 70 percent for two consecutive weeks, we proceed with the hardware purchase without relitigating the decision. That gives us a defined off-ramp rather than an indefinite deferral, and it means any purchase we do make will be sized against a better-understood demand curve.

I want to be honest about the uncertainty here. My utilisation estimates come from partial telemetry, and our demand forecast is extrapolation, not analysis. If anyone has data that contradicts the picture I've drawn — particularly on where peak load is actually going — I'd rather hear it Thursday than after we've spent the money or the quarter.

Please come with opinions. This is a decision we should make together, and the memo is a starting position, not a verdict.
